explain.say: Put a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in hot soup. A minute later, which one is too hot to touch? The metal one! Heat races through metal by conduction, which means passing energy along through a solid. Let us see how.

explain.say: Look at the first stage. The flame heats one end of a metal pan. The particles there start to vibrate, or jiggle, faster. Now see the second stage: each jiggling particle bumps the next one, passing the energy along. Is this fast or slow?

explain.say: On its own it is quite slow. But metals have a secret: free electrons, tiny charged bits that are not stuck to any atom. Look at the third stage. They zoom through the metal and carry energy far, fast. Does wood have free electrons?

explain.say: No, it does not, so wood is an insulator, which means it lets heat through slowly. Look at the last stage: in a metal pan, energy quickly reaches the handle. That is why many pan handles are covered with plastic or wood. Clever, right?

faq.a: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a solid as vibrating particles pass energy to their neighbours.

faq.q: Why are metals good conductors of heat?
faq.a: Metals have free electrons that move through them and carry energy quickly, as well as vibrating particles.
An insulator is a material that lets heat pass through slowly, like wood, plastic, wool or trapped air.

faq.q: Why do pan handles have plastic covers?
faq.a: Plastic is an insulator, so heat from the hot metal reaches your hand very slowly.
asks: Why are pan handles made of plastic?

faq.q: Why does metal feel colder than wood?
faq.a: Metal conducts heat away from your skin quickly, so your hand cools fast and it feels cold, even at the same temperature.
asks: Why do metal things feel cold?

facts: Copper conducts heat thousands of times better than typical wood.
Metals conduct heat well because of their free (delocalised) electrons.
